objectives: Read a throttling error and choose a mitigation
Decide whether provisioned throughput is justified
keyIdeas: On-demand is pay-per-token against shared capacity, with per-model, per-region quotas on requests and tokens per minute.
ThrottlingException is normal under load. Handle it with exponential backoff and jitter, not by retrying immediately.
Provisioned Throughput buys dedicated capacity at an hourly commitment — worth it only at sustained high volume.
Cross-region inference profiles spread load across regions and are usually the cheaper answer to capacity pressure.
misconceptions: That throttling means you did something wrong. It means the shared pool is busy.
That provisioned throughput is the default fix for throttling. It is a commitment; try inference profiles and backoff first.

concepts.title: Logging and observability
concepts.summary: You cannot debug or cost-attribute what you did not record, and Bedrock does not record it by default.
objectives: Enable invocation logging and choose what to capture
Identify the metrics worth alarming on
keyIdeas: Model invocation logging is opt-in and writes request and response data to CloudWatch Logs or S3.
CloudWatch metrics cover invocation counts, latency, token counts, and throttles.
CloudTrail records control-plane calls — who changed model access or guardrails — separately from inference.
Logged prompts and completions may contain sensitive data. Decide retention and access before switching logging on.
misconceptions: That logging is on by default. It is not, and the data is unrecoverable after the fact.
That capturing everything is the safe default. Prompt logs are a data-protection surface.

concepts.title: Bedrock cost model
concepts.summary: Partner-operated means separate pricing, and several AWS-only line items.
objectives: Estimate the cost of a Bedrock workload
Name the cost lines that do not exist first-party
keyIdeas: Bedrock has its own published per-model pricing, distinct from Anthropic's first-party rates.
Extra line items: Guardrails evaluation, knowledge base storage and retrieval, provisioned throughput commitments, and data transfer.
Caching works and still saves, but compute the savings at Bedrock rates rather than reusing first-party arithmetic.
Cost allocation tags and AWS Budgets are how you attribute and cap spend.
misconceptions: That Bedrock is cheaper because it is bundled with AWS. It is priced separately and may be higher or lower.
That the token counts differ. The tokens are the same; the rates are not.

concepts.title: Network isolation and data flow
concepts.summary: Where the bytes go, and how to keep them off the public internet.
objectives: Design a network path that keeps Bedrock traffic inside AWS
Explain what a VPC endpoint policy adds over IAM
keyIdeas: An interface VPC endpoint (PrivateLink) lets resources in a private subnet reach Bedrock without a route to the internet.
Endpoint policies restrict what can be called through that endpoint — defence in depth alongside identity policies.
Data is encrypted in transit; customer-managed KMS keys cover the stateful features such as knowledge bases.
Understand the data-handling terms for the model provider you use before sending regulated data.
misconceptions: That a VPC endpoint alone secures access. It controls the network path; IAM still controls who may call.
That private networking changes what the model provider may do with the data. That is a contractual question, not a network one.

concepts.title: Production architecture on Bedrock
concepts.summary: Putting it together: a real service that streams, retries, observes, and does not leak credentials.
objectives: Design an end-to-end Bedrock architecture for a streaming user-facing feature
Place the trust boundary correctly
keyIdeas: Clients never hold AWS credentials. They call your endpoint; your compute holds an execution role with a narrowly scoped Bedrock policy.

Streaming to a browser or app usually means API Gateway with WebSockets, Lambda response streaming, or a container behind a load balancer — plain synchronous Lambda behind REST fits long generations poorly.
Handle throttling with backoff and jitter; consider a queue for anything that need not be interactive.
Instrument from the start: token counts, latency percentiles, throttle rate, and cost per request, tagged per feature.
misconceptions: That Lambda is always the right compute. Long streaming generations bump into timeouts and payload limits.
That the execution role can be broad because it is server-side. Least privilege limits the blast radius of an injection.

concepts.title: Where credentials live
concepts.summary: The first architectural decision in any AI product, and the one most often got wrong.
objectives: Place the trust boundary correctly for a client application
Explain what a thin backend proxy buys beyond hiding the key
keyIdeas: A client application must not hold a provider credential. Any key in a binary is extractable.
The standard shape is a thin backend that holds the key and exposes only the operations your product needs.
That proxy is also where per-user rate limiting, spend caps, abuse detection, and audit logging live — none of which a raw key allows.
This app deliberately breaks the rule: it is a single-user personal tool with keys in the Keychain. That tradeoff does not survive contact with a real user base.
misconceptions: That obfuscating or encrypting an embedded key helps. The app must decrypt it, so an attacker can too.
That the proxy is only about secrecy. Its real value is control: limits, quotas, and an audit trail.

concepts.title: Latency you can feel
concepts.summary: Perceived latency is a design problem as much as an engineering one.
objectives: Reduce perceived latency for a described feature
Identify which levers change real versus perceived latency
keyIdeas: Stream. Time-to-first-token is what users experience; total duration matters far less than it feels like it should.
Real levers: a smaller model, lower effort, shorter outputs, fewer chained calls, and prompt caching on the prefix.
Perceived levers: streaming, optimistic UI, showing reasoning summaries, and doing work before the user asks.
Long agentic runs need progress feedback, or a correct result arriving in four minutes reads as a hang.
misconceptions: That a faster model is the only lever. Output length and chain depth usually dominate.
That caching mainly saves money. On long prefixes it is also a large latency win.

concepts.title: Retries and idempotency
concepts.summary: A retry policy that retries the wrong things turns a blip into an outage and a bill.
objectives: Write a production retry policy
Explain why jitter matters
keyIdeas: Retry 429, 5xx, and connection errors. Never retry 400, 401, 403, or 404 — they will fail identically forever.
Exponential backoff with jitter. Without jitter, every client retries in lockstep and you rebuild the thundering herd.
Respect retry-after when present rather than inventing your own interval.
A timed-out request may have completed and been billed. Cap total attempts and total wall-clock, not just attempt count.
misconceptions: That more retries mean more reliability. Past a small number they amplify an incident.
That a client-side timeout cancels server-side work. It does not, and you may pay for the result you discarded.

concepts.title: What to record
concepts.summary: You cannot debug, cost-attribute, or improve a system whose calls you did not record.
objectives: Design the logging schema for an LLM feature
Decide what must not be logged
keyIdeas: Per request record: model, token counts from usage, cache hit fields, latency, stop_reason, and a correlation ID.
Aggregate: cost per feature, p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate by type, refusal rate, and cache hit rate.
Sample full prompts and responses rather than logging everything — enough to debug, not enough to become a breach.
Prompt and completion logs are a data-protection surface. Decide retention, access, and redaction before you enable them.
misconceptions: That logging the response text is enough. Without usage and stop_reason you cannot explain cost or truncation.
That a falling cache hit rate will announce itself. It is silent unless you chart it.

concepts.title: Retrieval augmentation
concepts.summary: Getting the right context in front of the model, which is mostly a retrieval problem rather than a prompting one.
objectives: Design a retrieval pipeline and identify its weakest stage
Explain why answer quality is usually bounded by retrieval
keyIdeas: The pipeline is chunk, embed, store, retrieve, rerank, assemble. Generation is the last and usually least interesting stage.
Chunking strategy dominates quality. Chunks that split a fact from its context cannot be recovered by any prompt.
Hybrid retrieval — keyword plus vector — beats pure vector for names, identifiers, and exact terms.
Evaluate retrieval separately from generation, or you cannot tell which half is failing.
misconceptions: That a large context window makes retrieval unnecessary. It changes economics, not relevance — irrelevant context still degrades answers.
That better prompting fixes bad retrieval. If the fact is not in the context, no prompt recovers it.

concepts.title: Documents and images in production
concepts.summary: Real inputs are PDFs and screenshots, and they bring their own failure modes.
objectives: Build a document pipeline with verifiable answers
Handle the size and page limits
keyIdeas: PDFs and images go in as content blocks; the block type must match the MIME type.
Limits are real: 32 MB per request and 600 pages (100 on 200K-context models). Split larger documents deliberately.
Citations turn 'the model said so' into a verifiable span with a page or character offset — worth enabling wherever a user might dispute an answer.
Scanned documents without a text layer depend entirely on the model's vision; quality varies with scan quality.
misconceptions: That a PDF is just text. Layout, tables, and multi-column flow all affect extraction.
That citations are optional polish. For anything consequential they are the difference between an answer and a claim.

concepts.title: Refusals and failure UX
concepts.summary: Models decline sometimes. What your product does next is a design decision you should make on purpose.
objectives: Handle a refusal gracefully in a user-facing flow
Distinguish a refusal from an error and from a bad answer
keyIdeas: A refusal is HTTP 200 with stop_reason 'refusal' and a populated stop_details. Error handling will not catch it.
Decide the product behaviour: rephrase, route to a human, degrade, or explain. Silence is the worst option.
On some models a server-side fallbacks parameter re-runs the request on another model within the same call. It is not available on Bedrock.
Log refusal category and rate — a spike usually means a prompt change, not a change in users.
misconceptions: That refusals are rare enough to ignore. At volume they are a routine code path.
That a refusal means the user did something wrong. Often it is your prompt or retrieved context triggering it.

concepts.title: Approval gates and blast radius
concepts.summary: Autonomy is a dial, and where you set it should follow from reversibility.
objectives: Classify a set of actions by reversibility and assign gates
Design an approval flow that people will not reflexively click through
keyIdeas: Classify actions by reversibility and blast radius. Reversible and local: automate. Irreversible or outward-facing: gate.
Outward-facing actions — sending mail, posting, paying, deleting — deserve a gate regardless of model confidence.
An approval that shows no meaningful detail trains people to approve reflexively, which is worse than no gate.
Prefer reversibility over approval where you can build it: dry-run, staging, soft delete, and undo scale better than human attention.
misconceptions: That a confident model reduces the need for gates. Confidence is uncorrelated with the cost of the mistake.
That more approvals mean more safety. Approval fatigue converts a control into a formality.

concepts.title: Controlling spend
concepts.summary: Free wins first, then the levers that trade quality — in that order, always.
objectives: Produce a ranked cost-reduction plan for a described workload
Explain why the ordering of levers matters
keyIdeas: Free wins first: prompt caching, trimming dead input tokens, shorter outputs, removing redundant calls, and batch where latency allows.
Then quality-trading levers: lower effort, a smaller model, tighter output caps — each validated against an eval.
Measure before optimising. Most bills are dominated by one route, and intuition about which is usually wrong.
Guard with limits: per-user quotas, per-feature budgets, and alerts on spend rate rather than monthly totals.
misconceptions: That switching to a cheaper model is the first move. It is a quality trade, and caching often beats it outright.
That a monthly budget alert is sufficient. By the time a monthly total fires, the money is spent.

concepts.title: Versioning prompts and models
concepts.summary: Prompts are production code. Treat them like it.
objectives: Set up prompt versioning with a rollback path
Explain why prompt changes need release discipline
keyIdeas: Keep prompts in version control, reviewed, with the eval run in CI on every change.
Pin the model explicitly. An implicit or floating model is an unversioned dependency in your hottest path.
Log which prompt version and model produced each response, or you cannot investigate a bad output after a deploy.
Roll out prompt changes gradually where the surface allows it — the failure modes are not always visible in aggregate.
misconceptions: That a prompt change is low risk because it is only text. It changes behaviour as thoroughly as a code change.
That you can reconstruct which prompt produced a past response from git history alone. Log the version with the response.

concepts.title: Defending an agent with tools
concepts.summary: Injection stops being a curiosity and becomes an incident the moment the model can act.
objectives: Design layered defenses for an agent that reads untrusted content and has write tools
Explain why no single layer is sufficient
keyIdeas: Map every path untrusted text takes into the context: user input, fetched pages, documents, tool results, other agents.
Least privilege on tools is the strongest layer. An agent that cannot delete cannot be talked into deleting.
Add approval gates on consequential actions, validate tool arguments in code, and constrain outputs to schemas.
Monitor for the signature: sudden unusual tool sequences, or actions unrelated to the stated task.
misconceptions: That instructing the model to ignore embedded instructions is a defense. It raises the bar slightly and is not a boundary.
That input filtering solves it. Injection can be encoded, indirect, or arrive through a tool result you did not filter.

concepts.title: Capstone: ship something real
concepts.summary: Design, build, evaluate, and cost an agentic feature end to end, on both providers.
objectives: Ship a working agentic feature with an eval, a cost model, and a threat model
Defend every significant design decision
keyIdeas: Start from the four agent criteria and justify the tier you chose — a workflow is a legitimate answer.
Build the eval before tuning. You cannot claim an improvement without a baseline.
Instrument cost and latency from the first request, not after the bill surprises you.
Write down the threat model: what untrusted input reaches the context, and what the worst action the system can take is.
misconceptions: That the capstone is about building the most sophisticated thing you can. It is about defending your choices with measurements.

concepts.title: Escalating to a stronger model
concepts.summary: The advisor tool lets a running agent consult a stronger model at the moments that matter, instead of you picking one model for the whole task.
objectives: Decide when an agent should escalate rather than continue
Pair an executor and advisor model correctly
keyIdeas: The advisor is a server-side tool: Claude calls it mid-task and applies the guidance before continuing. You choose the advisor model; Claude chooses the moment.
It receives the full conversation including every tool call and result, so it is answering with the same context the executor has — not a fresh summary.
The natural moments are before committing to an approach, when stuck on a repeating error, and before declaring a task done.
The advisor must be at least as capable as the executor. An invalid pairing returns a 400.
This is the alternative to running the whole task on your most expensive model: pay for strength at the few points where it changes the outcome.
misconceptions: That you decide when the advisor is consulted. You choose the model and the availability; the executor decides when to ask.
That escalation is the same as just using the stronger model throughout. The point is spending capability where it changes the decision, not everywhere.

sources.title: Escalate hard decisions with the advisor tool

concepts.title: Plugins and marketplaces
concepts.summary: A plugin bundles skills, agents, hooks and MCP servers into one installable unit, so a working setup can be shared rather than described.
objectives: Install a plugin and choose the right scope for it
Decide when your own configuration should become a plugin
keyIdeas: Installing a plugin adds its skills, agents, hooks and MCP servers to Claude Code at once — it is a bundle, not a single capability.
Scope decides who gets it: personal, project, or organization. A project-scoped plugin means a new contributor's Claude Code is configured by cloning the repo.
Plugins come from marketplaces, which you add by URL. Anthropic publishes some; you can host your own.
A plugin is executing code with access to your context, and its hooks run on your machine. Installing one is a trust decision, not a preference.
Plugins have dependencies and versions, so a setup that works can be pinned and reproduced.
misconceptions: That a plugin is just a bundle of slash commands. It can carry hooks and MCP servers, which run code.
That installing from a marketplace implies review. Treat a third-party plugin the way you would treat any dependency you are about to execute.

concepts.title: The Bash sandbox
concepts.summary: Instead of approving every command, you declare which files and domains commands may touch and let the operating system enforce it.
objectives: Configure a sandbox boundary for a real project
Explain why an OS-enforced boundary beats per-command approval
keyIdeas: You define the filesystem paths and network domains commands may reach; the OS enforces that for every Bash command and its child processes.
The prize is removing approval fatigue. A learner who clicks through fifty prompts an hour is not reviewing anything, so the prompts were buying nothing.
Enforcement is by the operating system, not by the model's cooperation — the distinction that makes it a boundary rather than an instruction.
It runs on macOS, Linux and WSL2. Native Windows is not supported; run inside WSL2 there.
A boundary drawn too wide is theatre. Scope it to the project and the hosts the build genuinely needs.
misconceptions: That the sandbox makes an agent safe to leave unattended. It bounds the blast radius of shell commands; it does not review what the agent decides to do inside those bounds.
That fewer prompts means less control. Per-command approval that people reflexively accept is weaker control than a boundary that holds without attention.

concepts.title: Parallel sessions with worktrees
concepts.summary: A git worktree gives each session its own working directory, so two agents can work on one repository without overwriting each other.
objectives: Run two sessions on one repository without their edits colliding
Choose between worktrees, subagents and separate sessions
keyIdeas: A worktree is a separate working directory with its own branch, sharing the repository history and remote. Edits in one never touch another.
This is the isolation mechanism for parallel *sessions*. Subagents split work inside one session and share its working directory.
Pick by what needs isolating: file edits need worktrees, context needs subagents, and neither is a substitute for the other.
Cross-session messaging lets sessions in different worktrees pass findings to each other.
Parallelism has a review cost. Three branches produced in an hour still need one human to read three diffs.
misconceptions: That subagents give you parallel file editing. They share the session's working directory, so concurrent edits collide.
That more parallel sessions means more throughput. The bottleneck usually moves to review, not generation.

concepts.title: Routines: agents that run without you
concepts.summary: A saved prompt, repository set and connector set, run on a schedule, an HTTP call, or a repository event — on infrastructure that is not your laptop.
objectives: Decide whether a task belongs in a routine rather than a session
Design a routine whose output is reviewable
keyIdeas: A routine packages a prompt, repositories and connectors once and runs it automatically on managed cloud infrastructure, so it does not need your machine awake.
Three triggers: a schedule, an HTTP POST to a per-routine endpoint, or a repository event such as a pull request or release.
This is unattended execution, so everything from the headless lesson applies: budgets, scoped credentials, and output that lands as a pull request rather than a push.
